title: Geometric Alignment without Functional Equivalence: A Layer-wise Analysis of the Speech-Text Modality Gap
claim: High representational alignment between two input modalities in middle layers does not imply they function equivalently; their outputs diverge later.
layout: 3 columns: inputs left, two stacked plots center, answers right; arrows
description: A left-to-right schematic wrapped around a central framed panel. On the left, an orange box labeled Text holds a sample logic question, and a blue box labeled Speech shows a waveform. Orange and blue arrows lead into the central panel. The panel stacks two line plots that share a layer axis from 0 to 28. The top plot, Geometry, shows speech–text CKA as a teal curve that rises to about 0.6. The middle layers are shaded and labeled aligned in middle layers, and a dashed gray permuted-positions baseline sits near zero. The bottom plot, Function, shows answer margin for text (orange) and speech (blue). The two lines overlap until the late layers, where a gray shaded region marks them separating. On the right, arrows lead to an orange box with a check mark and the word correct, and a blue box with an X and the word wrong. The eye goes first to the two curves in the center.
caption: Geometric alignment without functional equivalence. The same question enters a speech LLM as text and as speech. Speech--text CKA is high in middle layers, yet the answer margins of the two inputs separate in late layers. Curves use Qwen2.5-Omni on BBH, with CKA from [ref] and margins averaged over the 233 items answered correctly only from text.
abstract: End-to-end speech large language models (LLMs) often answer the same question less accurately from speech than from text, even when the spoken content matches the text prompt. Existing analyses study this modality gap through the geometry of representations and measure how closely speech representations align with text. Geometric alignment gives the gap a measurable form, but it does not show whether the model uses aligned representations in the same way. This work connects representation geometry with answer formation and asks whether geometric alignment implies functional equivalence. We compare cross-layer Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) with layer-wise answer margins for four open-weight speech LLMs on SpeechMMLU and VoiceBench BBH. In Qwen2.5-Omni and MiniCPM-o, speech and text representations align in middle layers while their late-layer answer margins still differ, so mid-layer alignment does not imply functional equivalence. Qwen2-Audio instead shows weak alignment, which indicates a different failure mode. An attention intervention at fixed input and token count identifies a causal effect of late attention allocation on answer-code separation, a quantity distinct from answer correctness. Compressing the speech signal or its token sequence repairs a subset of the errors that occur only with speech.
